title: Amy Poehler Tells Noah Wyle ‘The Pitt’ Needs More Romance: If You’re ‘Gonna Show the Guts, You Gotta Show Some Butts’
description: Amy Poehler sat down with Noah Wyle on Tuesday’s episode of her “Good Hang” podcast to discuss both “ER” and “The Pitt” on the heels of his People’
body:
Amy Poehler sat down with Noah Wyle on Tuesday’s episode of her “Good Hang” podcast to discuss both “ER” and “The Pitt” on the heels of his People’s Sexiest Man Alive appointment. She also used her time with the actor to provide some feedback on the lack of romance in the latter of the hit medical shows.

	“You’re not asking me for feedback on ‘The Pitt,’ but I’m going to give you a little bit of feedback,” Poehler began. “If you’re going to show so much guts and blood, if you’re gonna go there — and your makeup team is incredible. The stuff you do is bananas. I don’t watch most of it. I cover my eyes, but I mean, I can’t take it — But if you’re going to show that much, every time you got to get a little smooch. Someone’s gotta do a little smooch.”
	

	Wyle, unconvinced, responded: “Oh, you think it’s one for one?” “One for one, just a tiny smooch,” continued Poehler. “Just one middle of the day [smooch]!” Wyle remained unmoved, though he did say that he would “maybe” discuss a “one-to-four ratio, but certainly not one to one.” Poehler concluded, “You gonna show the guts, you gotta show some butts.” (Wyle pointed out that they do show butts on “The Pitt,” just not in romantic contexts.)

	Wyle has played the disgruntled attending physician Dr. Michael “Robby” Robinavitch for two seasons of HBO’s drama “The Pitt.” His portrayal of the doctor won him the Golden Globe for best performance by a male actor in a television series, drama in 2026, and back-to-back Emmy awards for best actor in a drama series in both 2025 and 2026.
	

	 Season 3 of the hit medical drama is set to premiere in Jan. 2027 and will follow Dr. Robby’s first day back on the job after a three-month sabbatical at the end of Season 2.

	Watch the full “Good Hang” episode here.

schema.headline: Amy Poehler Tells Noah Wyle ‘The Pitt’ Needs More Romance: If You’re ‘Gonna Show the Guts, You Gotta Show Some Butts’

title: Politico Plans Live Video Coverage of Midterm Elections
description:
Politico isn’t leaving live video coverage of the midterm elections to the usual suspects.

	The political-news outlet will stream “Politico Electi
body:
Politico isn’t leaving live video coverage of the midterm elections to the usual suspects.

	The political-news outlet will stream “Politico Elections Live” on Tuesday, November 3, beginning at 9 p.m., with five of its top journalists analyzing real-time results. The program will stream on Politico.com and the Politico app and also via YouTube.

	The panel features Politico “Playbook” co-authors Adam Wren, Dasha Burns and Will Steakin, alongside Jonathan Martin, the senior political columnist,  and Alex Burns, the senior executive editor. The panelists will share more than race calls, drawing on the outlet’s reporting from around the nation, sharing what they are hearing from sources, and explaining to viewers what the results mean for the nation’s politics in weeks to come.
	

	“Election night is when Politico’s audience wants more than a scoreboard. Our reporters have spent this cycle in the states and in constant contact with the candidates and campaigns,” says Jonathan Greenberger, Politico’s global editor in chief, in a statement. “’Politico Elections Live’ puts our audience in the room with them as the results arrive, with a sharp read on what the night means now and for 2028.”The livestream will cap a cycle of midterm coverage that has seen Politico journalists travel across the country, relaying their findings in programming such as  “On the Road” with Jonathan Martin, presented by Meta, and “The Conversation with Dasha Burns.” Both have visited swing states as part of their reporting.  Politico has in recent months placed new emphasis on video podcasts in a bid to showcase its journalists, who often contribute to mainstream news outlets.

schema.headline: Politico Plans Live Video Coverage of Midterm Elections

title: Hasan Piker Sues Scott Jennings for $72 Million Over Out-of-Context Lynching Quote
description: Twitch streamer Hasan Piker sued conservative commentator Scott Jennings on Tuesday, alleging that Jennings had defamed him by misconstruing a quot
body:
Twitch streamer Hasan Piker sued conservative commentator Scott Jennings on Tuesday, alleging that Jennings had defamed him by misconstruing a quote to make it sound like Piker endorsed lynchings.

	On his own podcast on Aug. 11, Jennings played a mashup of clips of Piker, including one in which Piker referenced going “back to a better time when lynchings were happening.” Jennings denounced the commentary and warned Black voters of the “Piker plan of returning our country to lynchings.”
	

	In the lawsuit, Piker’s attorneys state that it was clear that Piker was mocking another person’s argument — not offering his own support for lynchings — and that Jennings repeatedly contorted Piker’s words to convey the opposite of his actual meaning.

	“These were not expressions of disagreement with Mr. Piker’s politics,” the lawsuit states. “Nor were they rhetorical characterizations of an admittedly controversial commentator. They were factual assertions about what Mr. Piker had said and advocated in his work. Each statement was demonstrably false.”

	The suit seeks $72.5 million in damages.

	Piker threatened to sue Jennings, who appears frequently on CNN, within a couple of days of the original comments. The controversy has already been adjudicated by Snopes, the myth-busting site, which came down on Piker’s side.

	“A full review of Piker’s unedited remarks confirms Jennings falsely claimed Piker said he was in favor of bringing back lynchings,” the site concluded. “In the original stream, Piker’s remarks on lynchings were sarcastic reactions to a user’s chat comment and opinions expressed by someone else in a separate video.”
	

	As a public figure, Piker would have to show that Jennings either knew what he was saying was false or that he acted with reckless disregard for the truth of the statements. He would also have to demonstrate that the comments were provably false statements of fact and not Jennings’ opinions.

	“Mr. Jennings was not simply expressing an opinion,” the lawsuit states. “He was falsely asserting that Mr. Piker had advocated racial violence against Black Americans.”

	Piker also asserts that he suffered harm to his reputation as a result of Jennings’ comments that damaged his ability to make a living.

	According to the complaint, Piker’s lawyers submitted a retraction demand to Jennings on Aug. 31, but they have not received a substantive response.

	The mashup of Piker clips had been circulated a few days before Jennings’ commentary by the National Republican Senatorial Committee. The compilation appeared intended to damage Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, who has appeared with Piker.

	“How does Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign surrogate Hasan Piker feel about Black Americans?” the NRSC asked on X. “Watch for yourself.”

schema.headline: Hasan Piker Sues Scott Jennings for $72 Million Over Out-of-Context Lynching Quote

title: Tokyo Opener ‘Sukiyaki’ Director Zeze Takahisa on the Protest Roots of a Global Japanese Pop Hit: ‘The Culture Used to Be Wide Open – Now It’s Become Narrower’
description: The opening film of the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival, Zeze Takahisa’s “Sukiyaki” tells the story of how the title tune became a worldwide
body:
The opening film of the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival, Zeze Takahisa’s “Sukiyaki” tells the story of how the title tune became a worldwide hit in 1963 as well as a beloved standard that has been recorded in foreign-language versions that have also topped charts.

	The film goes beyond the song itself to delve into the lives and careers of its makers: lyricist Ei Roksuke (Matsuzaka Tori), composer Nakamura Hachidai (Okada Junichi), and singer Sakamoto Kyu (Nakano Taiga). They became known in Japan as the “689 trio” with the unusual moniker coming from the “number” characters in their names: Hachi (8), Roku (6) and Kyu (9). But as the film shows in scene after highly charged dramatic scene, their professional and personal relationships were not always harmonious.
	

	Interviewed at the headquarters of Toho, the film’s Japan distributor, Zeze stressed the film’s relevance, six decades after “Sukiyaki,” known locally as “Ue o Muite Aruko” (I’ll Walk with My Head Up”), first hit the charts. “Back then the country was recovering from the war and all sorts of influences were flooding in from abroad,” Zeze said. “Those influences created an energy that propelled the popular culture here. Now Japan is absorbing fewer influences from abroad. The culture used to be wide open – now it’s become narrower.”

	But younger Japanese are now discovering that energy from the Showa Era (1926-1989), the period of Emperor Showa’s reign, when Japanese pop culture was at a fertile peak. Together with nostalgic Boomers, they could be found in the audience of “Godzilla Minus One,” the 2023 smash hit Godzilla series installment set in the early postwar period . The follow-up by director Yamazaki Takashi, “Godzilla Minus Zero” is also at TIFF as the festival’s Centerpiece screening, “It’s a kind of Showa boom,” joked Zeze.
	

	In casting “Sukiyaki,” he says, the main criterion was not a physical resemblance to its main characters, though Nakano Taiga channels Sakamoto’s exuberant stage persona with an uncanny precision. “It was more about the feeling the actors projected,” Zeze explains. “But Taiga comes from a show business family with roots in film’s period so he had a natural affinity for the role. Also, when Sakamoto sings in the film, it’s Taiga’s voice you’re hearing – he has an amazing talent as a vocalist.”

	The film’s drama, though, centers more on Nakamura and Ei, who joined forces to compose a series of hits in the 1960s but quarreled and parted as Nakamura spiraled into alcoholism. “ Nakamura went through a tough period after ‘Sukiyaki’ became a hit so we show that,” says Zeze. “If the film were just a success story, it wouldn’t be interesting – it has to have both ups and downs.”

	None of this drama had much to do with “Sukiyaki” becoming a hit abroad, but the film also delves into the sources of its creation, from Nakamura’s mastery of the jazz piano, which he displayed in New York clubs, to Sakamoto’s roots into early rock – he was a big Elvis fan – and Ei’s composition of the poignant Japanese lyrics,

	“Of course people abroad didn’t understand the lyrics, but the song’s energy came across to them,” says Zeze. “The lyrics reflect what was happening in Japan at that time.” Ei Rokusuke, the lyricist, was inspired by the demonstrations against the Japan-US Security Treaty in 1960. “ The demonstrators called for peace, but failed to stop the treaty ratification. “He wanted them to ‘walk with their heads up,’ despite their defeat,” says Zeze. “So the song has depth – it ‘s not just a cheery pop tune.”

schema.headline: Tokyo Opener ‘Sukiyaki’ Director Zeze Takahisa on the Protest Roots of a Global Japanese Pop Hit: ‘The Culture Used to Be Wide Open – Now It’s Become Narrower’

title: Melanie Lynskey to Play Erin Patterson in ‘Mushroom Murders’ Limited Series at Paramount+
description:
Melanie Lynskey is set to star in the limited series “Mushroom Murders,” which has been greenlit at Paramount+. 

	The show is based on the now-inf
body:
Melanie Lynskey is set to star in the limited series “Mushroom Murders,” which has been greenlit at Paramount+. 

	The show is based on the now-infamous case of Erin Patterson, the Australian woman who was convicted on multiple counts of murder and attempted murder after allegedly preparing food for guests containing toxic death cap mushrooms. The show will depict the 97 days between the meal and Patterson’s arrest.


	Lynskey will executive produce in addition to starring. Anya Beyersdorf (“Fake,” “Apple Cider Vinegar,” “Fires”), Daina Reid (“The Handmaid’s Tale,” “Shining Girl,” “Run Rabbit Run”) and Deb Balderstone (“Dustfall”, “Ticket to Paradise,” “Palm Beach”) created the series, all three serving as executive producers. Reid will also direct all six episodes. 
	

	Beyersdord will write along with Dianne Taylor (“Dustfall,” “After the Party”) and Belinda Chayko (“Dustfall,” “Fires”). Xavier Marchand also executive produces, as does Sophia Mogford for Paramount+. Soapbox Pictures will produce. 

	“This is an ambitious series that brings a gripping real-life story that captivated Australia and the world to the screen with the scale, quality and creative vision audiences expect from Paramount+,” said Beverley McGarvey, president of Network 10 and head of streaming for Paramount Australia. “It is a powerful addition to our growing slate of premium storytelling, and we are delighted to partner with such an exceptional creative team to share it with viewers around the world. We are also thrilled to welcome Melanie Lynskey, whose remarkable talent will be integral to the series both on screen and as an Executive Producer.”
	

	Lynskey currently stars in the Paramount+ series “Yellowjackets,” which is going into its fourth and final season. She has received two Emmy nominations for outstanding lead actress in a drama for her work in the series. She was also nominated in 2023 for guest starring in the hit HBO series “The Last of Us.” Her other TV credits include “Two and a Half Men,” the true crime drama “Candy,” “Togetherness,” and “Mrs. America.” 

	She is repped by Gersh.

schema.headline: Melanie Lynskey to Play Erin Patterson in ‘Mushroom Murders’ Limited Series at Paramount+

title: ‘Reacher,’ ‘Neagley,’ ‘Lioness’ Give Paramount TV Studios Three of September’s Four Most-Streamed Original Series
description: “Reacher” sure has some reach. The Prime Video series ended September as the month’s No. 1 original streaming series, according to Nielsen. “Reache
body:
“Reacher” sure has some reach. The Prime Video series ended September as the month’s No. 1 original streaming series, according to Nielsen. “Reacher” comes from Paramount TV Studios, which had a good month: The company’s “Reacher” spinoff “Neagley” was ranked third, tied with another Paramount TV Studios series, “Lioness.”

	“Reacher” hit the top spot with 4.6 billion minutes viewed, according to Nielsen’s streaming content ratings for viewers 2+ between Sept. 1 and 30, 2026.
	

	In second place for the month was Season 4 of Apple TV’s “Ted Lasso,” from Warner Bros. TV, which brought in 3.6 billion minutes of viewing.

	Then came “Neagley,” the Paramount TV Studios series that premiered its Season 1 in its entirety on Sept. 16. The Prime Video show received 3.3 billion minutes of viewership during the month — as did Paramount TV Studios’ “Lioness,” which airs on Paramount+.

	In fifth place was Netflix’s “Monster: Lizzie Borden,” which premiered Sept. 17 and grabbed 3.1 billion minutes of viewing.

	It’s been a solid fall for Paramount TV Studios, as its CBS series “Marshals” premiered Season 2 on Oct. 4 as the week’s No. 1 entertainment series among both broadcast and streaming for the week, according to live+7 multiplatform data.

	“Reacher” and “Neagley” both come from Paramount TV Studios and Amazon MGM Studios; Nick Santora is the showrunner on “Reacher” (which stars Alan Ritchson) and serves as co-showrunner with Nicholas Wootton on “Neagley” (which stars Maria Sten). “Lioness” (starring Zoe Saldaña) comes from Paramount TV Studios and 101 Studios; Taylor Sheridan is among the exec producers.

schema.headline: ‘Reacher,’ ‘Neagley,’ ‘Lioness’ Give Paramount TV Studios Three of September’s Four Most-Streamed Original Series

title: Punk Band Guitar Wolf Rocks Back Into Takeuchi Tetsuro’s ‘Wild Zero Overdrive’ at Tokyo Gap-Financing Market
description: Guitar Wolf, a real-life punk outfit with a long record of touring internationally, headlines “Wild Zero Overdrive,” director Takeuchi Tetsuro’s fo
body:
Guitar Wolf, a real-life punk outfit with a long record of touring internationally, headlines “Wild Zero Overdrive,” director Takeuchi Tetsuro’s follow-up to his 1999 film “Wild Zero.” 

	The project is among those at this year’s Tokyo Gap-Financing Market.

	Takeuchi said he is using the original as a template and updating it for the present day. “Precisely because we’re living in the age of AI, I want to convey the heat that comes from raw, primal punk rock,” Takeuchi said.
	

	The Japan-Canada project is produced by Takegei Company Limited. Takeuchi is putting together the budget with his own money as the base, while also searching for distribution partners. Casting is underway.

	“Rock’n’roll never dies. And love for Japanese subculture and rock’n’roll. UFOs. Motorcycles. Love,” Takeuchi said of what he wants audiences to take from the film.

	“I’ve been a huge fan of ‘Wild Zero’ (1999) ever since it came out. I even named my dog Ace, after the film’s main character.” said Toronto-based producer Takabatake Aki.

	Takabatake met the new film’s cinematographer by chance in Toronto, while Takabatake was working on a commercial, and took the encounter as a sign.

	“‘Wild Zero Overdrive’ and I are bound together by an unbreakable rock ’n’ roll pact,” Takabatake said.

	In Tokyo, the team will pitch the project to industry professionals at TGFM / Frontières Tokyo. The producers are also looking for further financing, distributors in Japan and abroad, and international sales agents.

	“Hopefully, we’ll be able to connect with some great potential partners who share our passion for the project,” Takabatake said.
	

	The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market runs as part of TIFFCOM, the content market attached to the Tokyo International Film Festival.

schema.headline: Punk Band Guitar Wolf Rocks Back Into Takeuchi Tetsuro’s ‘Wild Zero Overdrive’ at Tokyo Gap-Financing Market

title: Ancestral Memory Meets AI in Himalayan Drama ‘Shirjara: Song of Grandmother’ at Tokyo Gap-Financing Market
description:
A Himalayan drama that sets a grandmother’s stories against the rise of artificial intelligence is aiming for a Cannes premiere next year. 

	Direc
body:
A Himalayan drama that sets a grandmother’s stories against the rise of artificial intelligence is aiming for a Cannes premiere next year. 

	Director Bikash Subedi’s Nepali feature “Shirjara: Song of Grandmother” has wrapped principal photography and is at the Tokyo Gap-Financing Market to raise its last $44,000.

	Described as a speculative drama, the film moves between the traditional culture of the high Himalayas and a modern world shaped by technology. Its central question is what people building learning machines might gain from the knowledge of their ancestors – knowledge kept alive outside written archives and digital databases.
	

	“My earliest memories are of sitting beside an old hearth in the high Himalayas, listening to my grandmother tell stories. She was around 90 years old, and those moments left a deep impression on me,” Subedi said.

	As an adult surrounded by screens and data, he began asking why so much effort goes into teaching machines to understand people while humans still have so much to learn about themselves. That question gave rise to the film. “For me, this is a personal journey from the motherboard back to the marrow,” Subedi said.

	The shoot took place at roughly 4,000 meters in Dhorpatan, Nepal, on the Arri Alexa 35, and the team has assembled an 80-minute rough cut.

	Producer Subash Bhusal of Kingdom Network Pvt. Ltd. said the altitude created real logistical hurdles. “But we believed the story was worth the effort,” Bhusal said.

	The film carries a total budget of $296,000. Kingdom Network has already raised and spent 85% of it, leaving a 15% gap for finishing. That money will cover DI color grading, picture finishing, the master DCP and a custom six-minute AI and VFX sequence tied to what Subedi calls his AnI Cinema, short for Ancestral Intelligence.
	

	“I am not against technology. I am interested in what happens when we bring technology into a deeper conversation with our own history and humanity,” Subedi said.

	In Tokyo, the team wants to bring Japanese partners on board as co-producers and for post work. It also hopes to sign a sales company to handle international rights and to find distributors across Asia, with an eye on launching the film at Cannes in 2027.

	“For us, supporting ‘Shirjara’ was an opportunity to back a filmmaker with a distinct perspective and to bring a deeply rooted Nepali story into a wider international conversation,” Bhusal said.

	Subedi is already developing the next installment in his AnI Cinema movement, a project about ancient trans-Himalayan trade routes and memory across time. Kingdom Network also has further projects from Asia in development, each grounded in a specific local culture.

	The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market runs as part of TIFFCOM, the content market attached to the Tokyo International Film Festival.

schema.headline: Ancestral Memory Meets AI in Himalayan Drama ‘Shirjara: Song of Grandmother’ at Tokyo Gap-Financing Market

title: Variety Nominated for 62 Arts & Entertainment Journalism Awards
description: Variety has amassed 62 nominations for the Los Angeles Press Club’s 19th annual National Arts & Entertainment Journalism Awards, including nods for
body:
Variety has amassed 62 nominations for the Los Angeles Press Club’s 19th annual National Arts & Entertainment Journalism Awards, including nods for Print Journalist of the Year for Chris Willman and Online Journalist of the Year for Ethan Shanfeld.

	In the criticism category, Owen Gleiberman was nominated for film critic (over 1,000 words) as well as music critic and Daniel D’Addario was nominated for theater/performing arts critic. Willman was nominated for music critic, online columnist of the year and print columnist of the year, among other nods. 
	

	Several Variety cover stories were recognized as finalists, including Daniel D’Addario’s Jodie Foster cover, Trish Deitch’s Jamie Lee Curtis cover, Shanfeld’s Miley Cyrus cover and D’Addario’s Charlie Hunnam cover. 

	In the art and photography category, Daniel Doperalski was nominated in the portrait photo, music/theater/arts category for his photo for Variety’s “KPop Demon Hunters” cover. 

	Shanfeld was also nominated for several other reported features; his “Baywatch” casting call story is up for TV Industry Feature (Over 1,000 Words), while his investigation into the Diddy trial “circus” is up for Music/Performing Arts Industry Feature (Over 1,000 Words).

	Winners will be revealed at the Art & Entertainment Journalism Awards on Dec. 6 at the Biltmore Hotel in Los Angeles, where Brandi Carlile will be honored with the Humanitarian Award. Variety won 20 prizes at last year’s Arts & Entertainment Awards.

title: Horror Film ‘The Land of Jinn’ Is First Indonesia-Kyrgyzstan Co-Production, Unveiled at Tokyo Gap-Financing Market
description: Indonesia and Kyrgyzstan have made their first film together. “The Land of Jinn,” a supernatural horror feature directed by Kevin Rahardjo (“Smothe
body:
Indonesia and Kyrgyzstan have made their first film together. “The Land of Jinn,” a supernatural horror feature directed by Kevin Rahardjo (“Smothered”), was unveiled at the Tokyo Gap-Financing Market as the first co-production between the two countries.

	The story centers on a young Indonesian woman who journeys to Kyrgyzstan in search of a mystical healer who might save the baby she is carrying. Along the way, she unwittingly ties her child’s destiny to the jinn that roam the region. The film draws on the story of King Solomon, said in legend to have commanded the jinn.
	

	Makbul Mubarak (“Autobiography”) and Tumpal Tampubolon (“Crocodile Tears”) wrote the screenplay.

	“I’ve always been fascinated by the lengths someone might go to in pursuit of what society tells us is a ‘complete’ life, and what drew me to this project was the chance to translate that desire into the language of horror,” Rahardjo said.

	The journey takes the protagonist to Kyrgyzstan’s frozen, snowbound mountains. “The landscape is more than a backdrop. It becomes part of her obsession, beautiful and unforgiving, and almost indifferent to human desire,” Rahardjo said.

	Cameras rolled in Kyrgyzstan’s Issyk-Kul region and in Jakarta. The film, in English, Indonesian and Kyrgyz, is now in post-production, with a release planned for 2027.

	Yulia Evina Bhara and Amerta Kusuma produce for Jakarta-based KawanKawan Media, while Sultan Pirzhan and Elvira Sarieva of FreeMinds and Maksat Bolotbek of Bairak Group produce on the Kyrgyz side.

	“I think fear is universal, but ghosts are local,” Bhara said.
	

	She noted that people in both countries live alongside the unseen world, and that children in each grow up hearing their grandparents’ warnings not to venture out after Maghrib, the sunset prayer. “In Indonesia we have 17,000 islands and 17,000 ghosts. In Kyrgyzstan, the mountains and steppes have their own Jinns,” she said.

	She pointed to the complementary strengths of the two industries, with Kyrgyzstan offering auteur talent, unspoiled scenery and a door into markets across Central Asia and Eurasia, and Indonesia bringing a proven horror market, a 65% local market share and a profitable model for the genre.

	“This project was an incredible start to what will hopefully be a long lasting creative collaboration between Indonesian and Kyrgyz filmmakers,” Sarieva said.

	Also on board as a producer and delegate is Nazira C. Noer, CEO and co-founder of film marketing and publicity firm Poplicist, whose clients have included “Jumbo,” “Agak Laen” and “Ghost in the Cell.” She is also Navvaros Entertainment’s chief marketing officer and serves as secretary general of the Indonesian Film Agency.

	In Tokyo, the producers want to find partners to close the film’s financing gap and handle distribution, with the goal of locking in pre-sales or a festival route for 2027. Bhara also hopes to present the film as a template for co-productions within Asia.

	Rahardjo’s next project is a creature feature unfolding in a countryside village in Indonesia.

	The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market runs as part of TIFFCOM, the content market attached to the Tokyo International Film Festival.

title: Demi Lovato Hospitalized After Possible Allergic Reaction, Quickly Discharged
description:
Demi Lovato
                          Hospitalized After Potential Allergic Reaction
body:
Demi Lovato
                          Hospitalized After Potential Allergic Reaction
                          ... She's Doing Fine
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                October 27, 2026
                
                            2:14 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  October 27, 2026
                                3:23 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Demi Lovato had a scary start to her week after suffering a possible allergic reaction that landed her in the hospital ... but TMZ has learned she's doing just fine.
      
    
            Demi gave fans a glimpse of the ordeal on Instagram Monday night, sharing a photo of herself with an IV in her arm and a hospital wristband.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            She wrote, "sooooo i'm either allergic to passionfruit or sushi now!"
      

            The singer didn't elaborate on what symptoms she experienced ... and didn't mention any possible triggers other than the passionfruit and sushi.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Sources with direct knowledge tell TMZ ... Demi didn't stay overnight and was discharged shortly after checking in to be evaluated. We're told her symptoms subsided pretty quickly.
      
    
            Demi later reassured fans with a follow-up Instagram Story, writing, "i'm fine!!"
